content:
This is my first post on here so let me know if this is not the right place for this kind of thing.

I recently found an AI-generated Lean proof of Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture through minimum outdegree 8 (improving the previous bound of 7): https://github.com/RyanChimienti/seymour-eight.

I'm finding that there's not a great process for "submitting" something like this as a hobbyist and I'm curious if people here have any advice. Some more details:

  • It's a huge unwieldy case analysis (143k lines and 5.5-hour build time) that probably does not contain much strategic insight.
  • A brief attempt to incorporate comparator failed, I think because the proof is so heavy that it ran out of memory.
  • Palomar seems unpromising since the proof makes heavy use of bv_decide, which I've learned introduces axioms that Palomar does not allow. Plus, its acceptance test uses comparator and would probably hit the same memory consumption issue I did.

I am personally not in much doubt about the correctness of the proof because:

  1. I've read the formal statement of the theorem carefully and I'm confident that it means what it claims to.
  2. There are no sorry or axiom keywords in the code.
  3. I imagine any trickier loophole to fake a proof would have to be embedded intentionally, and I don't believe that a modern AI would quietly do such a thing when it was instructed to produce a real formalization. (But maybe the Lean experts here can say otherwise?)
  4. I had the AI develop the proof in a Python project first, and the AI was satisfied of its correctness there, so it has passed muster in two fairly independent contexts.

Of course, while (3) and (4) are strong evidence from my perspective, I realize that to anyone else they basically amount to "trust me bro."

Congratulations!

I don't know there's One True Path right now, everything's in the air at the moment. In their defence scale is a problem all its own! I will say that already you've done far more for reproducibility than people used to give for published computationally-assisted results, but the goalposts are always moving. :upside_down: Even without Lean, lots of papers prove an algorithm, run it in a faster language, and then register the code and results.

Frankly even if you didn't have the Lean backup like you do, like Terry's wrestling with in his IEANTN project (https://github.com/teorth/IEANTN/blob/main/GRAPH.md) there are going to be degrees of support for different claims for the foreseeable future,so I don't think that should be a blocker.

1) You've recorded things so if it matters to you priority arguments shouldn't be a concern at this point.

2) That said math people do prefer to cite papers, even un-refereed ones from the arxiv which gets special treatment, rather than other sources like repositories or Zenodo (if it's not for a raw data source). So you could draft a short note explaining your methods reducing the problem to your calculations, which people could cite. Various journals cover SNC work if you wanted to formally submit something.

3) You could get out your (AI-powered) pruning shears to try to reduce the overhead of the implementation (as distinct from the algorithm): there's definitely some redundancy there. Also changes which separate the raw data for the branches from the branch logic itself would be cleaner. Seems unlikely to me you'd be able to cut it down enough but who knows?

3b) You could also use your numerically-found constraints to switch to more a more feasible-region, or full-on theorem-based approach which could cull a lot of your cases and make it more Palomar-friendly. It's a lot easier to cut things down to size when you have a working model already! This seems like a good route to a v2, with your v1 priority already secured.

4) In full transparency I tried part of 3b myself wondering if I could iterate on your work to push it to 9. Didn't land there yet, partly because I'm so memory-constrained I can't run the original, so instead I got distracted going in a different direction trying to set up degree-independent theorems. Did manage to close the already known 1-5 cases, which is something I guess?

I'm not an expert in that conjecture. As a hobbyist you still need to make sure this is novel, by analyzing the literature that cites the paper of the conjecture. You cannot fully rely on LLM there because, esp. with older papers, the PDFs are behind paywalls and not accessible by LLM. That's your homework before announcing something.

Thanks @Douglas McNeil for the encouraging reply!

Adding a paper is a good idea. The question is whether I have the motivation to interpret the Lean proof well enough, write it up, and find an Arxiv endorsement. What I would really like is a more permissive Palomar, which catalogues Lean-only proofs but allows them to exist in a "we couldn't check it" state, and/or uses user voting as a signal of valid proofs. Or--this would be really cool but probably years away from a technical standpoint--let users build their own Lean code and just submit a SNARK as proof that it built.

Agreed that the implementation could do with some better code reuse, and I should have the AI do some cleanup passes on that. I'm doubtful that I can get the runtime and memory usage much lower, since I've already squeezed the AI in that direction. Build time was actually 15 hours at first, and it took many rounds of optimization to get it down to 5.5. (Interestingly, there is a fairly consistent tradeoff where the cases can be split into finer cases, which reduces the peak RAM usage but increases the total build time.)

As far as pushing the result to 9 goes, I suspect it would actually be pretty easy if you were able to dedicate a powerful computer to it full-time for a few weeks. The task feels like it's compute-bound instead of intelligence-bound. It's all just waiting for SAT solvers to finish, and if they take too long or use too much RAM, the AI splits the case into easier subcases and tries again. But I totally empathize with getting distracted chasing bigger fish--it's just crazy what's possible right now. I swear every third prompt I'm getting some original and elegant result...

@Ralf Stephan re: novelty, I've been through the literature manually and am confident that it's novel. Or at least, if someone else proved it, they did so very recently and have not yet publicized it widely.
